newsitem.title: INDIA: India's rulers, Congress in bid to avert polls.
newsitem.headline: India's rulers, Congress in bid to avert polls.

text.p: India's ruling United Front coalition and its Congress Party foes launched a last-ditch effort on Friday to avoid fresh elections by finding a successor to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, leaders of both sides said.
They said a consensus candidate for the top job could be named by the United Front before a parliamentary vote of confidence scheduled for later on Friday, or more probably afterwards.
"We are expecting a change in leadership," Hannan Mollah, a deputy of the Communist Party of India-Marxist, told Reuters after Deve Gowda moved the confidence motion in the lower house.
"There is an awareness that the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has to be fought together."

Bitter foes during the general election campaign last year, the 15-party United Front and Congress joined hands after the polls to put an abrupt end to the right-wing Hindu nationalist BJP's 12-day stint in power.
Congress deputies said a deal was being hammered out to replace Deve Gowda in an attempt to avoid elections, which politicians said could be held by June if the impasse continued.
"Either before the vote or after, a new leader will be chosen," said Jayanthi Natarajan, a Congress deputy. "We believe the United front has already named its candidate."
Shankarsinh Vaghela, chief minister of Gujarat state and a BJP dissident, said: "A new leader will be chosen...We will not have elections."

Speculation centred on G.K. Moopanar, a former Congress member who left the party last year and joined the United Front, and the chief minister of Andhra Pradesh state, Chandrababu Naidu. But Naidu said he was not a candidate.
United Front leaders said they would not abandon Deve Gowda before the vote, expected around 1430 GMT, but would hold a stock-taking meeting after parliament took its decision.
Asked if the United Front would try to strike a deal with Congress, coalition spokesman Jaipal Reddy said: "That will depend on the meeting in the evening."
Congress president Sitaram Kesri initially staked a claim to power, but later said he would settle for the replacement of Deve Gowda with a new leader.

Expectations that the centre-left coalition and Congress would be able to back a joint candidate to replace Deve Gowda pushed up share prices on Friday. The Bombay bourse's key index ended up nearly one percent.
News that parliament was expected to hold a special session on April 21-23 to take up the budget also spurred a rally in stock prices. The budget was announced in February.

The speaker of the lower house, P.A. Sangma, held a meeting with leaders of political parties early on Friday to discuss the fate of the budget. "There was general consensus that the budget should be passed," a participant in the meeting said.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said he was confident the investor-friendly budget for fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) would be passed despite Deve Gowda's difficulties.

Congress sparked the political crisis on March 30 when it abruptly withdrew support for Deve Gowda, saying the prime minister had tried to sideline India's oldest party and failed to stand up to the BJP.

Deve Gowda's alliance of regional, left-wing and centrist parties controls 178 votes in the 542-member lower house of parliament. Congress has 140 votes, while the BJP and its four allies control 193.
